big: Rohan's car gets a ₹30,000 dent. His insurer pays ₹25,000, not ₹30,000. The ₹5,000 difference is not a mistake. It is a word on the first page of his policy.

lines: Why did the insurer not pay the full bill?
Most likely the deductible. It is the part you pay yourself before the insurer pays. Learn four words and your policy stops being a mystery.

rows: Sum insured is the most it can pay
note: A higher deductible usually means a lower premium, but you carry more of each small loss.

title: Insurance words
stops: The premium is what you pay to keep the policy in force
The sum insured is what you pay at each claim
A deductible is the part of a loss you pay yourself
A policy renews itself with no premium
caps: You pay the premium to keep the cover alive.
The sum insured is the most the insurer will pay.
The deductible comes out of each claim before the insurer pays.
Renewal needs the premium paid before the policy lapses.

q: Meena's repair bill is ₹40,000 and her deductible is ₹10,000. What does the insurer pay?
why: ₹40,000 would ignore the deductible she has agreed to carry.
₹10,000 is her own share, and not what the insurer pays.
The insurer pays the bill less her deductible: ₹40,000 less ₹10,000.
₹50,000 adds the deductible to the bill, which is wrong.

opts: The premium that Rohan pays every year
The amount of tax saved on the premium paid
The commission earned by the agent who sold it
why: It is the upper limit of what the insurer will pay for a claim.
The premium is what Rohan pays. The sum insured is what he can claim.
Tax savings, if any, are a separate matter from the sum insured.
An agent's commission is not related to what the policy pays.

q: Meena forgets to renew her policy and the date passes. What may happen?
opts: It continues for another term at no cost
The policy may lapse, and cover can stop
The insurer pays double at the next claim
The sum insured grows to make up for it
why: A term continues only if the premium is paid on time.
Renewal needs the premium before it lapses, or cover stops.
No insurer pays double for a missed renewal.
A sum insured does not grow on its own, whatever happens.

q: Rohan picks a higher deductible to cut his premium. What is the trade-off?
opts: A higher premium and a much bigger payout
No change in what he pays or in what he gets
The insurer pays his deductible for him each time
A lower premium, with more paid by him
why: A higher deductible does not raise the premium or the payout.
It changes both what he pays each year and what he pays at a claim.
The point of a deductible is that he pays it himself.
A larger deductible lowers the premium, but he bears more of every loss.

pts: The premium keeps the policy in force. Renew before it lapses.
The sum insured is the most the insurer will pay.
A deductible is the part of a loss you pay yourself.
